utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we understand this point. What I want to do is just to 23 put these records in before the Court at this stage. We 24 understand the purpose of your testimony on this matter. If we 25 just look at the next document dated 21st July '93, and it is 26 patrol sheet 019/-95? Again it refers to Sergeant Desimir 27 Grujicic and states on 21st July 1993 they were ordered to 28 patrol facilities and routes indicated in the Prijedor region. Again the purpose was the apprehension of the conscript Dusko Tadic and remand to the Unit's deployment area pursuant to the order of the Battalion Commander of 19th July 1993. That is the order they got, but if we look at the next document we indicated we can see how it impacted upon you, because it states that you were apprehended on 21st July 1993. Is that right, that on 21st July 1993 that was another occasion as part of your enforced mobilization that they had arrested you? 10 A. Yes. 11 Q. Thank you. 12 A. Here you can see there the region to be searched around Kozarac and Prijedor. I would always go to my workplace in Kozarac. When I spoke to the Secretary in the municipality, who was in charge of all the Secretaries of the Local Commune, he said, "You have to report there in the specific time of the day", but it was a circle because whenever I would show up at work I was afraid that I may be arrested, and often times it did happen that I was arrested. So I wanted to move somewhere else, to another -- in the school there were a lot of rooms. I was persecuted. I was not aware of what was going on. Sometimes when I would come to Kozarac my neighbours would say, "The military police was looking for you". I was surprised because they could have found me, but often they were looking for me. This time I know that I was taken to Slatina in a luxury car. It was a zastava model 101. 28 Q. If we look at the next document dated 9th August 1993, again we 1 see a patrol sheet, again it is Sergeant Desimir Grujicic and we 2 see the order for the apprehension of the conscript Dusko Tadic 3 upon the orders of the Battalion Commander of 5th August 1993. 4 That is the order. If we look at the next document beneath it 5 we can see a note related to the completed assignment and, "The 6 individual was taken into custody on the premises of the Fire 7 Brigade in Prijedor, and after the interview with the personnel 8 or personal officer, Gavrilovic, the individual escaped".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember this event very well. At the time my wife was 10 already abroad in Germany, and I was in Prijedor by myself with 11 my mother and I was living in an apartment above Jugo-Banka. 12 I remember in the morning I went to find medicine for my mother, 13 gangrene of a toe, and I saw the police van approaching. At 14 first, I did not know who they were looking for. Then Desimir 15 beckoned to me. I turned around and started to run, and he 16 started running after me. I remember jumping over a fence, two 17 fences, and he was jumping over after me. I came to a wall and he said, "Stop or I will shoot." 19 I turned around and I really saw him. He was holding a gun. 20 Maybe I would continue running ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I could stop you here. We do not need this detail as it 22 is not that crucial for the case. The facts are spoken of 23 within the documents and I do not think the Court would object 24 if I interrupted you on that matter. If we look at the next 25 document that is dated 30th August 1993, we again see the same 26 order. Again it is Sergeant Desimir Grujicic and the order of 27 30th August 1993, "shall patrol the facilities, routes, areas 28 indicated below, Prijedor, Pecani, Kozarac", and the assignment 1 is to remand the conscript Dusko Tadic pursuant to an order of 2 28th August 1993. If we look at the last page, which is a final report, 4 it says, on the completed assignment, but it says, "The 5 conscript Dusko Tadic was not found at the indicated address or 6 seen in the Prijedor or in Kozarac. He was sought at regular 7 intervals and has not been found". What I would like to ask you 8 about is this. That reviews those documents. You referred to 9 your wife being in Germany during this period. Can you tell us 10 why she left for Germany during this summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, we were not clear about the main reasons were my 12 arrest. We simply could not survive there any more together. 13 At moments it seemed to us that it was because I got this cafe 14 to use, and it was a Major of the army of Republika Srpska was 15 behind it, but it was not the real reason. I took some 16 confidence in thinking that was the only reason, but when I was 17 taken to the fire station, when my wife had already gone abroad, 18 it was then that I realised that the difference -- that the 19 reasons were very different and after that interview at the fire 20 station I fled and I never went back. I only once went back while I was in Banja Luka. It 22 was at night. I visited friends in Prijedor, and I asked them 23 what to do and they said it was best for me to leave and not to 24 come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did your wife leave the area to go to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She left after -- before this arrest on 9th August, and after my 27 arrest of 21st July, somewhere in that period. I am not sure, 28 but I know that I saw them off to Belgrade. I returned and I was arrested promptly. So that was the very end of July. 2 Q. Did you go to Germany as well? 3 A. I went to Germany in November from Belgrade. 4 Q. Between August and November where were you? 5 A. I was in Banja Luka, hiding at my brother's, and I was staying there during the day, but I was afraid that they would come and look for me there. So I was sleeping at his mother-in-law, at Milosa Duica Street, with Ljubo's son Nenad. He was keeping me company there, even though he was living with the brother. 10 Q. What was your reason then for going to Germany in November 1993? 11 A. After my arrest in the fire station, I knew that I could not survive in Prijedor. Major Gavrilovic, he is the one who interrogated me. It was not just an interview, it was not just an interview; it was an interrogation, and at that time I realised that I had to leave the Prijedor municipality as soon as possible and go as far as possible. I did not know that I would go to Germany. I did not want to stay in the Republika Srspka. Gavrilovic told me openly, he knew -- he had all the information about the brothers, "You are no warriors, you are no soldiers". He was mocking us. "They were good in karate but they do not fight". Now he had all the information. In general, he cited the reasons. I remember signing a few documents after the interrogation. At first, he said that he would take me to Radio Prijedor to publicly apologise to the Bosnian Serb Army because I had said that they were a private army. I showed him the document that I had work obligation. He said, "I will check it 1 with Slavko Budimir", and he said, "Yes, this is a legal 2 document, but we will revoke it today", and he said, "No, no, 3 you will stay here", and then I was detained. There was a detention unit in the fire station, and he 5 said, "You are going to sign that we are not a private army, 6 that you will sign that you were a representative of Muslims". 7 Then I remembered that it was during the period of time when 8 I was taking part in the civic forum activities, and I told him 9 that I was coming to Prijedor with a group of citizens that had 10 nothing to do with any power or government. I was not connected 11 to them. He said, "No, no, no. You negotiated on behalf of 13 people who later turned against the Serb authorities", and 14 I said that I would sign that I was a member of this delegation, 15 but I did not know the background of all this. I could not have 16 known. I did not know if there was somebody who wanted to 17 manipulate me. He said, "It was only formal negotiations. You 18 were really preparing for a war". So I said that I would sign. He said, "I will let you 20 go if you sign". Then he said, "I cannot let you go, but if 21 people from the military police let you, you can go to your 22 mother's". I heard, overheard, when he gave the order for the 23 van to be prepared and for me to be taken to the front. Somebody told me, "I did not know what is going on. I do 25 not know where they are taking you, but you will be killed on 26 the front". So, in August, the unit where I was was not on the 27 front line. At that time I realised for the first time the 28 seriousness of what was going on, and I told to a soldier, the last salary, the last money that I had, I gave to this Desimir so that I could be allowed to take medicine to my mother. I had about 50 Marks. I ran into the apartment, my mother's, grabbed all the documents that I had and fled towards Banja Luka. I went on foot to Petrov Gaj where I knew that the priest Majkic lived. So I stopped there for a coffee. A train arrived and that is how I got to Banja Luka. All in all, I went on foot. I did not use the same road. When I would hear vehicles, I would go into the fields. When I came to the priest, I know he was surprised at how I looked. I was filthy and sweaty. I did not tell him what had happened. I was embarrassed. I just told him that I was going to Banja Luka and I did not tell him what was going on. When I was in Banja Luka later, I called some of my friends and asked them what was going on. I had a telephone number of somebody in the military police, Riki Lekenic, and he told me not to go -- leave Banja Luka, that he would come to Banja Luka and tell me what was going on. 20 Q. Did you go to Munich in Germany? 21 A. I first went to Nuremberg and then my brother Mladen came to Nuremberg and took me to Munich. 23 Q. Did you stay in the house of your brother Mladen in Munich? 24 A. I lived in the same apartment as he did for a certain period of time. It was a studio, and then I moved to a room which was part of his club, and that is where I lived. That is where I lived with my wife and my two children. 28 Q. When you were in Munich is it right that you were arrested on 12th February 1994 by the German police? 2 A. Yes. 3 Q. Subsequently, you were interviewed by investigators for the Prosecution Office of the Tribunal on 9th to 10th May 1995? 5 A. Yes. 6 Q. And 21st to 22nd December 1995? 7 A. Yes. 8 Q. That is all I have to ask you. If you could remain there? 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Cross-examination, Mr. Tieger? 10 MR. TIEGER: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, may I ask the Court for the Court's indulgence for a brief recess? I was having a document attended to by the translation unit which, I think, will expedite matters considerably. It has not arrived and I will check on its progress. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Do you expect that you will have it or do you need a recess to check on its progress? Hopefully to check on its progress but also to have it, I gather? 18 MR. TIEGER: Correct, that is right. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Five minutes. 20 MR. TIEGER: May I have 10? 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We will stand in recess for 10 minutes. 22 (10.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24 (10.40 a.m.) 25 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, are you ready to proceed? 26 MR. TIEGER: Yes, your Honour, thank you. 27 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We have to keep them satisfied. We try very hard. You may proceed. 1 MR. TIEGER: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3 Q. In your testimony you spoke about the good people of Kozarac, predominantly Muslims. Those good people, at least most of them, are not there any more, are they? 6 A. Yes. 7 Q. They were driven from their homes? 8 A. Well, probably some of them were chased away and some left of their own will, but not all of them have been chased away. 10 Q. Many were rounded up and put into camps, isn't that right? 11 A. I do not know what your question is. 12 Q. Many of the Muslims from Kozarac and from opstina Prijedor were rounded up by Serbian forces and put in camps? 14 A. I did not take part in any of such activities. 15 Q. But you were aware that that was happening in opstina Prijedor in the spring and summer of 1992? 17 A. Well, when I first visited Kozarac I did not find my neighbours there. At that moment I did not know what had happened to them. 19 Q. The religious buildings of the Muslim community were all destroyed? 21 A. During my first visit I saw that some had been destroyed and later when I came back to work as the Secretary of the Local Commune, yes, it is true that all religious property in Kozarac was destroyed. Many of them were also destroyed in Prijedor although there was no war there. 26 Q. By the time you left opstina Prijedor, about 90 per cent of the Muslim community of the entire opstina had been killed, forced out or thrown out, is that not true? 1 A. I do not know what the percentage would be exactly. I did not have any conversations about that. I am not very well informed of the percentage. 4 Q. Was the vast majority of the Muslim community of opstina Prijedor forced out of the area? 6 A. Probably some were forced and some left of their own will because they simply could not survive there any longer. There were several reasons, but many of Serbs also left the area. A great percentage left the area for different reasons, economic reasons, and simply because they did not want to take part in the war. 12 Q. What happened to the Muslim community of opstina Prijedor was done under the direction of the authorities of the new opstina Prijedor? 15 A. I do not know whether it was under their orders. 16 Q. Those new authorities were comprised of persons who wanted and created a Srpski, Serbian opstina Prijedor and a Serbian Kozarac? 19 A. The intentions were not clear to me, the intentions of the new authorities, whether it was about creation of Republika Srpska within Bosnia or something else, I do not know. I was not aware of -- I did not know about the intentions of those authorities. They were not made public. You could only guess, assume, and I assumed that they themselves did not know. 25 Q. You mentioned in your testimony on Friday, I believe, in response to a question from your attorney, that you did not conduct the plebiscite in 1991 on behalf of the SDS, because the plebescite was conducted through the Skupstina Opstine, through the elected local assembly, on behalf of the whole opstina? 2 A. Yes. 3 Q. Can the witness be presented with Exhibit 146, please? I am sorry, that may be the wrong number. Your Honour, the Court may know this Exhibit. It is the decision on the plebiscite which was displayed in Court on October 25th. 7 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: How many hundreds of Exhibits do we have, 149? I do not know. I do not have the list of Exhibits before me. 9 MR. KAY: I think it is 146. 10 MR. TIEGER: That is what I have it listed as well. May I see the Exhibit for the moment and make sure that we are talking about the same one? That is the correct number, thank you. Sir, this document, the decision on appointment of voting officials for the plebiscite, is headed as the "Instruction for the Plebiscite of Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina", is that correct? 17 A. No. 18 Q. Can you look at the top of the page and see what that instruction indicates? Is that not pursuant to paragraph (2) under (4) of the instruction for the plebiscite of Serb people? 21 A. Yes, there was an instruction, but this is not the instruction on the plebescite. Here it says, "pursuant to paragraph (2) under (4) instructions for the plebiscite", so it is based on the instruction, was this decision issued. 25 Q. This particular decision? The appointment decision itself, although it cannot be seen on the monitor at the moment, is written in Cyrillic, is that correct? 28 A. Yes, the decision. 1 Q. There is a stamp at the bottom? 2 A. Yes. 3 Q. What does that stamp say? 4 A. "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, municipal board, Prijedor". 6 Q. You indicated in your testimony that the plebiscite itself was conducted in the churchyard of the Serbian Orthodox church because, you said, you did not want the plebiscite conducted in a private home and "there were no other communal objects". In fact, there were a variety of communal objects and buildings in Kozarac, but the Orthodox church was the only exclusively Serbian communal object, isn't that right? 13 A. No, the Orthodox church in Kozarac is over 120 years old, and all people visited, not only the church but also the churchyard, Muslims, Croats and others. I remember. I grew up there. We used to play football there. We spent a lot of time there in the churchyard, not only of the Orthodox church, but of the mosque as well -- me and my neighbours. 19 Q. So the mosque was a communal object or building, the Mjesna Zajednica was a communal building, the post office was a communal building? 22 A. Yes. 23 Q. But the Serbian Orthodox church was the only Serbian communal building? 25 A. Yes. 26 Q. As a matter of fact, it was the main board of the SDS which entrusted you with the responsibility to conduct the plebiscite? 28 A. No, not the main board, the municipal committee. At that time in the municipality of Prijedor there was a government which did not belong to any party, and the municipal committee reached a decision, issued instructions, as to the way the plebiscite should be conducted. The municipal committee was not composed only of members of the SDS. I do not even know if there were any members of the SDS there. Maybe, I know that there was a Croat was a member of that committee. 8 Q. Before you left Prijedor, you prepared a report to the SDS about your work from 1990 to 1993, is that right? We have seen that document in evidence. 11 A. On 8th, 8th August, I prepared that document in Kozarac and it was composed on the basis of various sources, sources of information, and various reports. 14 Q. You sent that report to a number of different places and persons. For example, you sent it to the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, correct? 18 A. I had the intention to do so, but I simply had no time to do it. I sent the document on the same day, that is, on 8th August. I took it personally to the office in the town hall in Prijedor. I had one copy with myself, and that copy was sent by me at the end of August through Rajko Lekenic to Prijedor to the main board of the Serbian Democratic Party. So one copy should be with the SDS in Prijedor. 25 Q. You also prepared that work report to be sent to the President of the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, Radovan Karadzic? 27 A. Well, I was -- there were not many preparations there. I just did it within 20 minutes. I was sitting in the office in 1 Kozarac. I was afraid that I would be arrested. So I wrote it 2 on the basis of what I had seen in the office in Kozarac and on 3 the basis of some reports that I had there, on the basis of my 4 recollection. So I managed to compose it and I managed to write it 6 on a typewriter although I had never used a typewriter before. 7 So I managed to do it very quickly and to hand it over there, 8 but I do not think it was really sent anywhere. As far as 9 I know, I personally handed it over in the town hall in Prijedor 10 and Rajko Lekenic took it from Banja Luka to the main board of 11 the SDS in Prijedor, and I do not think that anything was sent 12 to any other address. There is another copy of that report 13 which is with me, and I took it with myself to Belgrade and then 14 to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Copies were intended, however, whether they managed to get there 16 or not, to go to, among others, the President of the Bosnia and 17 Herzegovina SDS? You typed that yourself, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But they were intended for many other addresses as well. For 19 example, Commission for the Security and Co-operation in Europe, 20 the Red Cross of Yugoslavia, to many other organisations that 21 I had visited. I showed that document to the representative of the 23 United Nations in Belgrade, because in October I had talks with 24 them. They received me and I showed that document to them. 25 They saw it and we talked, and then they referred me to the 26 Federal Executive Council and they told me that I should try to 27 exercise my rights there and ask about what had been happening 28 to me in Prijedor municipality. I also visited the International Red Cross which had its seat in Sremska Mitrovica at that time. I also went to the seat of the UNHCR in Belgrade. 3 Q. Excuse me. I think you have answered the question that was asked. In that report you said that in November 1991 the main board of the SDS in Prijedor municipality entrusted you with the task of organising the plebiscite for Yugoslavia? 7 A. I do not know whether it says so exactly, but I probably thought that it was so. It should not -- it is not necessarily correct. 9 Q. May the witness also be shown Exhibit 97, I believe? May the English be placed on the monitor, please? Can you bring that down just a little bit? No, I am sorry about the confusion. We want the first page of that document which is the ballot paper. This document depicts the two ballots which were used for the plebiscite, isn't that right? 15 A. I suppose so. It is not very legible, but I presume. 16 Q. Those ballots are headed "The Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina"? 18 A. Possible. 19 Q. The plebiscite was important to the SDS, was it not? 20 A. I do not know. 21 Q. Was it not a sign of loyalty to the Serbian cause to vote in the plebiscite? 23 A. I would not say so. 24 Q. Is it not true that Serbs were denounced as disloyal for failing to vote in the plebiscite? 26 A. I guess you could say so, but it was not a general attitude at that time. It was not publicly said that way. It was believed that it was perfectly normal and that it is the duty of citizens to vote at the plebiscite, that it was their civic duty. 2 Q. As a matter of fact, did you not denounce Serbs as disloyal for failing to vote in the plebiscite? 4 A. I thought that they are people who could not be trusted, loyal or not loyal. I do not know whether someone should be loyal to me. Maybe in a later period ---- 7 Q. Just as you ---- 8 A. --- certain things were made clear, so I could have an impression that those were the people who were not aware of their own desires, who did not have any specific attitudes about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the plebiscite. Just like many other people at that time, we, simple people, ordinary people, did not know much about things at that time. 14 Q. Did you not denounce Serbs for failing to vote in the plebiscite as being disloyal to the Serbian cause? 16 A. No, I did not denounce them, but until the end of 1993 some things were such that you could realise that those who did not know, who had not known, whether to take part in public gatherings or not, that those were people whom you could not trust for anything. They could not be trusted when it comes to the plebiscite in Bosnia and Herzegovina or other things. Those people probably took part in all kinds of plebiscites and referendums that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was strange because it was difficult to understand, because someone who would vote for a plebiscite for Yugoslavia could later vote for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that one should know what he really wants, whether you want a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, a Yugoslavia, whether you want to live in Bosnia, in Herzegovina or not. At least, such were the circumstances in which we were at that time. 3 Q. You were not denouncing people for intellectual contradictions; you were denouncing them for failing to vote in the plebiscite because in so doing they were declaring unmistakably which side they were on, is that not true? 7 A. Well, in a later period it became clear that they were on nobody's side. They were not on the side of the Serbs or Muslims. They were just pursuing their own interests. Those were such people. They were just sitting on the fence and they did not know what they wanted. From time to time, they would side with the most extremist part of the Serbian population and then later they would ally themselves with the most extremist part of other people. 15 Q. You wrote to President Karadzic and others that Goran Babic had refused to participate in the Serbian plebiscite, but voted (as did his whole family) at the referendum for the sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, declaring in unmistakable terms what side he was on. You wrote that, did you not? 20 A. Yes, I did write something similar, but the information that you have in that report is based on everything that had taken place before -- throughout '92 and '93. That is, on the basis of some reports that were accessible to me at the time, I was writing that report, and those reports were made during the sessions of the Local Commune Assembly in Kozarac, Executive Board of the Local Commune of Kozarac and so on. That is how people declared themselves. The Secretary of the Local Commune -- as the Secretary of the Local Commune, I was in charge of taking minutes of those sessions and meetings, meetings of the Council of the Local Commune, and on the basis of that I composed that document. It is not always -- it does not always represent my personal opinions, but it is also something that testified to what people thought at that time in that area. 6 Q. You told this Court that you made no distinctions between Muslims, Croats, Serbs and others, but in fact you denounced Serbs for various reasons for disloyalty to the Serbian cause and, as part of that denunciation, you made sure that authorities knew whether or not they were married to a Muslim or Croat? 12 A. No. 13 Q. In your work report did you not denounce Ljuban Lukic and, as part of that denunciation, did you not write to President Karadzic and others that he had been married to a Muslim woman? 16 A. I was not writing to Radovan Karadzic. I never had an opportunity to exchange any correspondence with him or talk to him and, as far as that information is concerned, it is based on the events that took place in the period between -- in the period when our Local Commune was constituted in Kozarac, exclusively on that basis, and the information that was in the written reports of the proceedings, and Ljuban Lukic, 10 minutes before the death of Ostoja Baltic, was in his company, and it is very likely that in some way he contributed to his murder. He was one of my assistants and he was killed shortly thereafter. What happened, I do not know, but it was discussed at the session of the Local Commune in Kozarac. Maybe because his wife had close relationships with the Suljo Suljic, he was a 1 known criminal, maybe that was the reason why people believed 2 that he was a man who is collaborating with all sides and 3 damaging ordinary people. I know that he was one of the people 4 who wanted the Local Commune of Kozarac to come back and he was -- he, therefore, perished as an innocent man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You wrote this work report. It was copied to the President of 7 the Bosnia and Herzegovina SDS, among others. You denounced 8 Ljuban Lukic and, as part of that denunciation, you made sure 9 that the main board of the SDS, that the President of the Bosnia 10 and Herzegovina SDS, and that all the other groups you sent it 11 to, including the chief of the public security station in Banja 12 Luka, knew that he was married to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody knew that without that information. I was not 14 disseminating this information. I just said who I sent the 15 whole report and that was in the report of the Local Commune in 16 Kozarac. This is something that I was part -- it was part of my 17 job. I was not deciding what was right or wrong. It does not 18 reflect my own view, what my thoughts, my views were. That is 19 known to the people with whom I talked. But, as a Secretary of 20 the Local Commune, I wrote what was there. I do not know why this person was denounced because he 22 continued to live in Kozarac in a Muslim house. He even -- his 23 house was not even destroyed. He lived in the worst part of 24 Kozarac. Now he moved to the centre of Kozarac and this person 25 continues to live there to date. He was in the police before, 26 he is in the police today. I do not think that I contributed to 27 his denunciation. Those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You denounced Brane Koncar and, as part of that denunciation, you also made sure that the information that he was married or had been married to a Muslim woman was included? That is in the report too. When you condemned Goran Babic, you made sure that the people to whom you were sending the report knew that his wife was a Croat? 6 A. That was well-known. There was enough information. Everybody knew who was who. Those are -- that is redundant information. Those are the facts that existed. I did not invent that he was married to a Croat. That was known and that was established. 10 Q. When you wanted to denounce the new policemen in Kozarac who had been, according to you, appointed by Dusan Jankovic, you also made sure that everyone to whom you were writing knew that they were all related to Croats and Muslims; that was part of the denunciation? 15 A. I think that they abused relationships that they had with Muslims and Croats by not treating them fairly. My brother was married, one to a Muslim, one to a Croat, and that is a fact too. 19 Q. But it is true that when you denounced the new policemen you made sure to put in that they were all married to Muslims and Croats? That is in the report, is it not? 22 A. If it is there, that is probably how it is. That was based on how things were. You could not say that somebody was not a Muslim if they were a Muslim or a Serb if they were not a Serb. That was well-known in Kozarac and elsewhere. That was not a secret. It is a different thing whether people abused their family relations for individual private gain. I was not in such a position. I think that through those family connections they had access to many things that Muslims did not have access to. Maybe at the time I did not understand that, but later I did. 3 Q. You were in contact with Serbs who had been in Kozarac shortly after the conflict. For example, you met Milan Vlacina in Kozarac on your first visit? 6 A. Yes. 7 Q. He had been in Kozarac shortly after the conflict was over. In fact, he had been there so soon after that he was there to see Muslims being taken by buses to Trnopolje and Prijedor? 10 A. He told me that, but I do not know whether his story is based on what he saw or what he heard. That, I cannot know, but that is what he told me. On that day when we sat down, we were drinking beer in my cafe and he told me that. I really cannot know whether that was true or not, but that is what he told me. 15 Q. In addition to knowing some Serbian soldiers who arrived in Kozarac immediately after the conflict was over, you knew some Serbs who participated in the conflict? 18 A. That was the only man that I saw on that occasion, the others that I met in passing, I did not know them. I do not know if I may have seen one or two other people but Kozarac was empty. It was abandoned. 22 Q. Then you continued to describe the events of that period of time to Mr. Reid on that occasion and on other interviews. In May, on May 10th in fact, you discussed your mobilization. I thought of him, yes, I had him in mind.
