It had no significance for me. I was not a conscript to take my military equipment with me, and that rifle I had was exclusively in the house. 8 Q. Then I asked you whether or not you received a camouflage uniform in addition to the SMB uniform from Kusota and you said "no"? 11 A. I do not understand your question. 12 Q. You told us earlier that you had only received an SMB uniform from Kusota along with a rifle, no camouflage uniform. 14 A. I think that is how it was, and the uniform that I got from my brother I did not consider it a camouflage uniform. I did not consider it anything. I do not know. 17 Q. Let me refer you and your attorney to page 47 of the May 10th interview with you and Mr. Reid. Reference is 26 through 28. You describe the weapon and how you came into possession of it from Kusota. Then you say that, "He came back carrying on his back a big bundle which was wrapped in linen". The investigator asked, "Sorry, a big bundle of what, weapons?" You said the following: "No, no. Later I saw that actually inside was a rifle, uniform, boots, the regular army, the regular equipment that is issued to a soldier, and also I remember that there was a classic uniform and that there were also boots, and there was also a uniform of mixed colours, yellow colours". So that was another uniform which you had in your possession in 1992? 1 A. I do not think so. I am not sure. I cannot say. I only looked at that equipment and then left it. Even the boots that I got were not my size. 4 Q. You agree that you told Mr. Reid that you received a camouflage uniform in addition to an SMB uniform when Kusota brought the bundle that you described? 7 A. I did not get the uniform that Mr. Reid thinks about, and I think that that is what Mr. Reid thinks about. The yellow thing I did not get from him. That I can say with certainty. Maybe I did not -- I did even say so, but it is not important whether I got a yellow SMB or something else. I know that the uniform that he brought I never used. 13 Q. Mr. Tadic, I would like to satisfy you that the words were not Mr. Reid's but were yours and, in fact, were not suggested by Mr. Reid who was simply asking you a question about what you received. So perhaps you would like to look at your exact words? May I have this marked for identification and shown to the witness, please? 19 A. There is no need for that. I believe you. What I am telling is what I know for certain. Maybe I have said that way, but I know that it was not so. I do not think that there was any significance. When Mr. Reid and I talked I was not accused of anything regarding uniforms. Even if I had 10 uniforms, maybe I would have said there was something like that. It was insignificant. I am not accused of having a uniform. 26 JUDGE STEPHEN: My recollection may be in error, but I thought the witness in evidence in chief said that in the bag there was the SMB and there may have been a camouflage uniform. Did he not say that? 2 MR. TIEGER: I checked the transcript, your Honour. I will be happy to read that exact portion as I found it. 4 JUDGE STEPHEN: Yes. 5 MR. TIEGER: Mr. Tadic, as a matter of fact, you had enough uniforms that you were giving them away. Do you remember giving one to Mirko Vidovic in June? 8 A. When I started working with the police, it was not a big problem for uniforms, the one that I described. There were some reserve uniforms, auxiliary uniforms, and I gave one to my wife's brother. I was not in a position to give them out to others. Whoever was in the reserve police had an opportunity to get a uniform. As far as that uniform is concerned, I said, as far as I recall, at the time when we talked, I did not consider it significant whether it was in a bag or somewhere else. I thought that it was insignificant as a question. 17 Q. You yourself wore a camouflage uniform at the checkpoint, in addition to your blue police uniform? 19 A. That uniform I wore exclusively when my uniform of the reserve policemen was being laundered. I did not have two summer uniforms for the reserve police. I got it from Vokic Radovan. I do not know the date, but I got it from him and the winter one I got at the police station in Prijedor. 24 Q. Referring your counsel to page 83 of the May 10th interview -- for the benefit of the interpreters, I am looking for the reference number, just below 85 -- on that occasion you were asked to describe the uniforms you wore at the checkpoint. You said the following: "As far as I remember, during June of 1992, I mostly, mainly, wore a multi-coloured yellow uniform. The top part and the down part was the same colour." Those were your words, right? 4 A. Yes, as far as I recall, sometimes I wore that kind of uniform too. In any respect, I had police insignia on all of them, regardless of whether it was a yellow or a blue one. On each of those uniforms on the shoulder there was an insignia. There was "police" insignia written. I really cannot say how many times in June I wore that uniform and another one, but those are the reasons. There were no other reasons why. That was the only reason why the laundering of uniforms. 12 Q. That is why you wore mainly in June your yellow camouflage uniform. Let me ask you some questions about ---- 14 A. It is possible that that was the reason. That was one of the reasons. 16 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, the one that Mr. Tadic said had an insignia on it, is that the one that his brother gave him? 18 MR. TIEGER: Mr. Tadic, did you hear the Court's question? 19 A. Yes. I understand that question. When I started working in the police in Prijedor, we all got insignia, the police insignia, especially the word insignia, that are very conspicuous. It is about 10 centimetres wide, half circled, blue background and white stitching in Cyrillic letters "Police". We also signed out to the blue berets with the insignia, a metal badge of the Republika Srpska. 26 Q. Mr. Tadic, how many times were you in Trnopolje camp in 1992? 27 A. I will try to remember. I think I was there five times. I do not mean the camp -- you talked about the "camp". I do not know what you mean under the "camp", but in Trnopolje I was about five times. 3 Q. Where in Trnopolje were you? 4 A. The first time I was with Jovo Samardzija, as I said earlier, over the weekend in June of '92. 6 Q. That was in the camp? 7 A. Pardon? 8 Q. That was in the camp? 9 A. I do not know. Please ask me specifically. I do not know what you mean under a "camp", so I am not in a position to answer. Is it the whole complex or was it the street that I was passing on? It is not clear to me what you had in mind. 13 Q. Were you inside or at the site of Trnopolje camp with Mr. Samardzija? 15 A. Could you please say specifically? If you show me photographs, there were some photographs seen here, and if you show me the photographs, I will show where it was. It is not a secret. Some people are saying that the camp was the school building, some say that it was the entire complex. So now I am not sure what they think when they say the "Trnopolje camp". So, please, if you can be very specific with your question? 22 Q. When you visited with Mr. Samardzija, were you on the grounds of what had once been the school? 24 A. No, never -- neither at that time nor later. 25 Q. Were you on the street which runs immediately in front of the school within the boundaries of where the former school was? 27 A. You mean in the summer of '92? 28 Q. At any time in '92? 1 A. No, not in the summer. I said I was there five times. In the summer of '92, I was exclusively only once with Jovo Samardzija and I know where I was and whom I met. I know that I saw then -- I saw people who I grew up with and that is what stayed in my memory. Hiba Hankic, my neighbour, and her husband, Salih, I greeted them; greeted with Gunjic Ferid and I talked to him -- he still lives in Prijedor today -- with Osman, Sahib Kulasic. They all asked me what happened. I did not know what was going on. 10 Q. Were those people free to leave the area they were in, the area of Trnopolje camp? 12 A. I do not know if they could leave. We did not talk about that and again I say I did not meet them at that space where you say. I met them in the street, and some I met in front of the ambulance in Trnopolje, the space in front of the ambulance, ambulanta. In 1992, I was never in the school yard of Trnopolje. 18 Q. Have you told investigators on previous occasions, either the German investigators or the Tribunal investigators, that Trnopolje was an open area and people were free to leave? 21 A. At that time when I visited with Jovo Samardzija, that was my impression. What happened later, I do not know. Whether the status change in the summer of '92, I did not go there. When I saw -- neither my neighbours told me that it was very difficult for them, neither did I get that impression. 26 Q. Please tell us the other four occasions when you were in Trnopolje and, please, you can tell us what part of Trnopolje you were in? 1 A. I know that once I was there officially. I do not know, again I cannot say the exact date, but it was the moment when the refugees from Trnopolje were going to Karlovac in organisation of the Red Cross, the UNHCR. That was the first time that I went there on official business as a reserve policeman. I stood by a bus and my job was to help in -- to the Red Cross in its activities. I know that there was a young woman who was reading names off a list. She was in front of the school building. People were passing by her one by one and were getting on the bus. I know that we -- I remember that we stayed almost all day. It was raining and I had a blue cape and Goran Babic, the Commander of the police station in Kozarac, was with us and about 10 other policemen who had similar duties. 15 Q. What about the other three occasions you were in Trnopolje, when were they and where were you? 17 A. It was all in the period between the fall, that is, the end of 1992. On one occasion I remember I went to Trnopolje. First, in Prijedor I met Adil Jakupovic's wife. We often visited more often, more often than this gentleman stated here. Every other day or at least once a week we visited each other in Prijedor. On one occasion when I went to his wife, to their house, she told me she was not at the old address any more. So I found her at another house that was closer, and she said that Adil went to Trnopolje with one of the sons. 26 Q. When was that? When did you visit Trnopolje on that occasion? 27 A. I believe that it was the end of October 1992. I cannot say with certainty, but I also know that it rained again and the 1 weather was pretty bad. We stood by a house up the road, up the 2 street, and we talked. I know that Zonjic -- he is also a 3 reserve policeman. He is a refugee from Bosanska Bojna. He was 4 with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When were you in Trnopolje on the remaining two occasions you 6 recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly the date. On one occasion I was there 8 with my brother. At that time I worked as a Secretary of the 9 Local Commune and he came to Prijedor with Hamdija, his friend. 10 They came from Banja Luka. That Hamdija had a friend in 11 Kozarac, and he said, "Oh, let me come along". He wanted to 12 find a friend of his. I think his name was Rega. I had heard 13 of him. He was a salesman. So we went together to Trnopolje. He talked to some 15 people and finally found out that this man had been in Slovenia 16 for quite some time. That was one time. Also, I went as a 17 Secretary of the Local Commune with Popovic Joso. I asked him 18 to give me a ride to Trnopolje, because before that in Prijedor 19 I got many messages from the Red Cross. I went to the International Red Cross and they gave me 21 about 20 messages of refugees. Somebody from abroad were 22 writing to people who were the natives of Kozarac, and the 23 representative of the Red Cross gave me those messages and he 24 said, "All these are for people from Kozarac, so there". I left 25 that with the policeman on duty whom I found there and we 26 returned, Joso Popovic and I. I think the policeman's name was 27 Petkovic. He was in the part where the restaurant used to be, 28 across the street from the ambulanta, the health clinic. I do not know if I ever went there again after that. I remember seeing Adil Jakupovic on later occasions in Prijedor, and he said that he never managed to go there, that he got registered with the International Red Cross. It was his intention because otherwise he could not leave Prijedor in a normal, regular manner. The only way would be something unofficial, through the military or if you get a letter of guarantee from abroad, the other members of the family would write to the International Red Cross. 10 Q. Mr. Tadic, just focusing on Trnopolje, what were you wearing on the occasions you were in Trnopolje other than the time you described being there as a reserve policeman or the time you visited with Mr. Samardzija? 14 A. I do not remember. Sometimes I -- I remember when I went there on official business I had a raincoat of blue colour. When I went with Adil Jakupovic, I do not remember what kind of uniform I had. On other occasions, I went in civilian clothes, normal clothes that you wear. It was the fall and so I know that it was warmer clothing. 20 Q. Were you armed? 21 A. On the occasion when I was doing -- I was on security detail for the International Red Cross, yes. 23 Q. You have indicated you have some trouble remembering the dates. You just know it was sometime between the fall and then you did not specify what time period. Do you know whether or not you were in Trnopolje in October? 27 A. I think that around October 1st those refugees left for Karlovac. My birthday is on October 1st, but I am not sure that it was on that very day. I think there were maybe -- or maybe it was 31st, maybe it was 2nd, maybe it was 1st. I am not sure about the date. 4 Q. Do you know whether or not you were in Trnopolje in November? 5 A. It is possible. As I said, I do not recall exactly because there were very brief visits, except for the time when I was there officially. Then that day I was there from morning till dusk. The representatives of the Red Cross handed out food to the refugees, but they could not give us any. We could not give food to the police and the military of the Republika Srpska. 11 Q. Do you know whether or not you were in Trnopolje in December 1992? 13 A. I do not remember. I am not sure. I know that I think I was there about five times altogether down there, but it was not the -- I never entered, though, the space, as you claim. The closest encounter with people there was in the street with people that I knew. As far as I know, people moved around freely in the street. I do not know what rules were there at the time. When I was there with Adil Jakupovic, I know that people moved about freely. 21 Q. Were you in Trnopolje in September? 22 A. As I said, from the fall, that is, during the fall, I was there about four times and once during the summer. I know my reasons. I know why I went there. I know with whom I had contact there. I cannot say exactly when I went there the first time. In fact, I know that when I was there on official business it was when part of the refugees were leaving. I think it was 37 or 38 buses that were leaving Trnopolje. As far as 1 the other visits, were all to the town of Trnopolje. Maybe they 2 had other rules there, but I was exclusively in the street and I 3 know with whom I talked and why I talked and I never went there 4 alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, with respect to the uniforms you wore when you were in 6 Trnopolje camp, Mr. Tadic, did you not tell the German 7 authorities that on four occasions when you were in Trnopolje 8 camp you were uniformed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that I said that. I did not think it was 10 important. I know why I went there and I know exactly with whom 11 I went and I know with whom I met there. I know that I was 12 there once officially and that was then. I cannot tell you the 13 exact date with certainty, but I know that I was there on that 14 occasion when those people were leaving Trnopolje for Karlovac. 15 I know there was a white van which was parked there. It was an 16 UNHCR van. I talked to a representative on that occasion and it 17 was a Frenchman, and I also know that there was a representative 18 of the Red Cross there. There was the Red Cross there who 19 visited me in my detention unit. He told me that, indeed, there 20 was a French representative of the Red Cross there at that 21 time. I would have never gone there officially had I not known 22 that there was an International Red Cross office there and that 23 the UNHCR was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Earlier we discussed the rifle and the certificate which was 25 placed in front of you which indicates the certification for 26 issuance of a rifle and ammunition. You stated that you 27 received this paper from your brother Ljubo in Banja Luka on the 28 date indicated there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that I requested a similar certificate in Prijedor. 2 I used to know a man by the name of Slobodan Bokan and I asked 3 him for a such a paper, and he did give me a certificate of some 4 sort, but the certificate that I have seen here, it is the 5 certificate that I was given by my brother in Banja Luka. 6 I tried several times to obtain a similar certificate in 7 Prijedor because I saw that many of my neighbours in Kozarac had 8 similar certificates, and Fikret Tulundzic showed the same 9 certificate to me, except there was not the "Territorial 10 Defence, Banja Luka", but the "Territorial Defence, Prijedor", 11 marked on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let us talk about that for a moment. In fact, you were asked 13 about that in an interview with Mr. Reid to be found at page 14 48. It is reference Nos. 30 and 31. That should be May 10th 15 interview. "Can you explain the following about that 16 certificate, Mr. Tadic?" "Yes, that automatic rifle stayed in 17 my possession and that same rifle was signed out when I was 18 assigned to the reserve traffic police. Now, as far as this 19 automatic rifle is in question, in April '92 I spoke to Simo 20 Miskovic and I told him about the rifle and asked him what 21 I should do with it and he told me that I should keep it until 22 the police comes asking for it. But at, by the end of April, 23 the local residents of Kozarac had been saying, or whether they 24 were just rumours, that all weapons, unauthorised weapons, to be 25 found in the houses will be seized, confiscated. So, on one 26 occasion when I went to Prijedor, I do not know exactly when, 27 I spoke to Bokan Slobodan who was a reserve military personnel 28 and I told him about it and then he gave me a certificate, just like that, an empty certificate, that I had been issued a weapon. And since I was not mobilized, the origin of the weapon could have caused problems, so somewhere, around the beginning of May, I filled out that certificate in my own handwriting and I put down my own name, so that it would serve me as a sort of guarantee regarding the origin of the weapon". First of all, those are your words, correct? 8 A. Yes, that is how it happened, but it is not the same certificate I have been talking about. I was given a certificate from him. I forgot. I did talk to Miskovic, but I cannot tell you it was the beginning of '91. I think it happened at the end of '91. 12 Q. That is not the certificate that you were examining which is Exhibit 148? 14 A. No, it is a similar certificate but the title was different. It read "Territorial Defence, Prijedor". The other one is "Territorial Defence, Banja Luka". 17 Q. So at the beginning of May you filled out two or you actually forged two similar certificates for this weapon? 19 A. I did not forge it. I do not know why you think that I forged it. The data on the certificate are OK. The number of the rifle was important, nothing else. There was a kind of guarantee certificate of the origin. The fact that my name was there -- well, I see no other way I could have done that. I did the same thing as many of my neighbours did, nothing special. None of us never hid weapons, neither did my neighbours hide their weapons from me. Later on they were openly carrying weapons. They talked to me about everything. I had no secrets with my real neighbours. The only thing is that I could not contact with people who had had a criminal record from before and who were dangerous for anyone there. 3 Q. So, apparently, then you were aware of Serbian civilians being armed by the SDS? 5 A. Why do you think it is clear? 6 Q. You did not see that? 7 A. No, I did not. There were all kinds of stories. I cannot deny that. There were stories that people, both from the SDA, SDS, the green berets, were being armed. There were all kinds of stories. Which of them were true, I do not know. It was obvious that people were armed and that they were obtaining weapons, whether individually or in some other way, that is a different story. 14 Q. Let us pursue this just a bit more, if we may? So in May 1995 you told Mr. Reid about the certificate you say you got from Slobodan Bokan, but you did not mention the certificate you received from your brother? 18 A. Nobody asked me about that. I had other certificates that my brother had given to me. I had a certificate to travel to Serbia, for Belgrade. It was a similar certificate. 21 Q. In Court you mentioned the certificate you received from your brother, but not the certificate you received from Slobodan Bokan? 24 A. Had someone asked me, I would have said that. 25 Q. That certificate was found in your house when the German authorities searched it after your arrest? 27 A. I do not remember what was there, but when I fled Prijedor I just took everything I could. I put them in a bag and left. 1 The same thing happened when I was leaving Banja Luka. I did 2 not know what to take until the very moment I was leaving for 3 Serbia. If my departure had been normal, I would have probably 4 not taken. I did not think it was something dangerous. Those 5 are the facts. I did not say that I did not have a rifle, that 6 I did not have a certificate. It was the certificate that was 7 filled out with me and I am not responsible for that. If you think it is a forgery, then it is a forgery, 9 but I was never really a soldier. It is true that a soldier is 10 mentioned there, but I have never been a soldier. If you think 11 that I was a soldier, well, please, you can check on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tadic, I only meant it was a forgery in the sense that 13 you are saying you filled it out rather than an official filling 14 it out. In any event, the Germans seized that document and they 15 interviewed you. They asked you specifically about that 16 document, a document which said you were a soldier, which said 17 that you had been issued an automatic rifle, which said that you 18 had been issued 300 bullets, which said it had been issued from 19 the Territorial Defence of Banja Luka, and they said: "Mr. Tadic, what about that document?" You said: "I do not 21 know anything about it", isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is true, according to the description you just gave, 23 but that is the way they described it. But my answer is, no, it 24 is true I was not given the certificate by the Territorial 25 Defence and I was not given the weapons by the Territorial 26 Defence. I was not a soldier of the Territorial Defence. That 27 is not true. What is true is that I filled out that certificate 28 and I was not asked about that. It is true that I was given a blank form and all other details, other all data, that I was a soldier member of the Territorial Defence, that is not true. On the basis of that paper, I do not know. I do not know how you reached the conclusion that I was a soldier of the Territorial Defence because of that paper. Such data should be found in the military book. Ever since I served my military duty, regular duty, in the JNA, I have not changed my military book and all the relevant information is there in my military book. 10 Q. The German authorities asked you about the certificate referring to an exhibit number and they asked you: "What about that document?" You said: "I do not know anything about it", isn't that what happened? 14 A. Yes, that is what happened. The description that they gave, I do not know anything about that. I did not receive the weapon from the Territorial Defence, and that was my answer. How they described it, I do not know anything about that. That is correct and that is true. 19 Q. Mr. Tadic, that interview was interpreted for you throughout the entire process of the interview, was it not, and after each question and answer you and your attorney were permitted to object to it or to add to it, if you wished and you signed off on that page, your signature appears on that page, isn't that all true? 25 A. Yes, it is true what you are saying, the fact that I had the right to add anything I wanted to, and I asked for something to be added. You can ask Mr. Sklebitz. I wanted his assistance to add something, something that I thought that had not been 1 adequately described. I am not saying that the certificate was 2 not discussed, but it was not presented in the same light as 3 I presented it here. The German authorities, when at the end 4 of '93 we talked about the case, they wanted me to give a 5 statement in the case of Zoran Zigic and I said, "I will accept 6 if you allow me to add what I think should be added to my 7 previous interviews". They said, "OK" and then we sat down and 8 they even asked a Minister of some kind to come there and he 9 gave his approval. But that policeman told me that we would first discuss 11 the case of Zoran Zigic and then we would later discuss what 12 I wanted to be discussed or to add. I agreed and then we 13 discussed the Zoran Zigic case. After that when it was -- when 14 we had to discuss our previous interviews, when I wanted to add 15 something, when I heard -- when he heard what I said, he said, "No, it is out of the question. You said everything you had to 17 say". So I was not given the opportunity to say during that 19 interview, I do not know anything about interpretation, but 20 there are quite a few things that are not correct. The very 21 title "Local Commune Territorial Defence", I do not think that 22 German authorities knew about things, that they knew what was 23 what. Their objective was just to question me for ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You speak some German, do you not, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so. I do speak some English now. I have 26 learned it in my cell, although I do not have much communication 27 with the outer world, but I can understand some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not speak to the guards at the detention facility in 1 Germany in German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did communicate with one of the guards sometimes, but before, 3 before my departure, when I knew that I would be transferred 4 here. Nobody talked to me before that. They would just tell 5 me, "Go back to your room. Do this or that". They just 6 communicated in that way. I sometimes asked them for help, but 7 it was not a correct attitude towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: However much German you speak, you certainly do speak enough, 9 would you not agree, to know the meaning of "Ich weiss nicht"? 10 That is not too complicated? You can say and understand "I do 11 not know" in German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand you. I did have an interpreter when 13 I talked to the German authorities -- that is beyond doubt -- 14 but I just said -- I just described the way they talked to me, 15 the way they behaved towards me. I know that Mr. Reid said if 16 there is anything I want to add that I would have the 17 opportunity to talk later on, and that is what I was told in 18 Germany. But they did not allow me later on to discuss 19 anything. I am not saying it is -- I do not claim that what 21 I would say later on would be completely true. I was just 22 trying to tell what I could remember. I am not saying here that 23 I did not make any mistakes. I do not think anyone can remember 24 all the dates. I was accused several times and ever since 25 summer '92, and they kept asking me, "Where were you on the 26 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th?" and so on, in the morning and in the 27 evening. I was not a robot and there is nothing I can say in 28 relation to that. 1 Q. I asked you earlier about Witness W and whether ---- 2 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, before you go on to Witness W, maybe 10 minutes ago you made reference to a certificate that the German authorities asked about, then much else was discussed. It is still not clear to me what certificate they were talking about. You referred to an Exhibit number and then there was a long discussion about something else. Maybe I missed it. 9 MR. TIEGER: No. I will try to clarify that, your Honour. Thank you. Just to clarify, the document the German authorities were referring to when they asked you about the certificate issuing you a rifle and 300 bullets is the same document that was seized from your home in Munich and the same document that we have looked at here in Court today, is that correct? 16 A. I did not see that document in Munich during the interview. I was described that document in a different way. There are certain things that are written there and that were described in their own way, but the reality was different. Whether they were thinking of this certificate or some other certificate, I do not know. That is why I said that I do not know what they were referring to. That is the way they described it; that I was issued the rifle by the Territorial Defence, for example, that I was a soldier of the Territorial Defence. Those were their questions. They did not show me the certificate and that is why I gave them the answers that I gave them. This is the first time I am hearing this story, the story that you told here. I have never seen that certificate, the way they described it, and I do not know which certificate they were talking about. 3 Q. Just so it is clear, sir, the interview with the German authorities which you signed which was contemporaneously interpreted states: "Exhibit 1.12.87", your Honour, which is the German number, "contains a certificate dated 4th May 1992 that Dusko Tadic had been provided by the 'staff of the Territorial Defence' with an automatic rifle AP and 300 rounds of ammunition. Mr. Tadic, what can you tell us about that certification?" That was the question, sir. That was the question to which you answered you knew nothing about it. 12 A. I do not know anything about it. I do not know whether I was issued with that rifle by the Territorial Defence staff and that was my answer. I was not issued that rifle. 15 Q. Mr. Tadic, I asked you earlier about Witness W and asked you whether or not he was one of those who told you that he participated in the conflict in central Kozarac. You responded that he did not. I would like to direct your counsel's attention to the December interviews, December 22nd, on page 24 -- I am sorry, I apologise, page 69. That should be in the May series, on May 10th. Mr. Tadic, you were talking at that time on May 10th about the conflict in opstina Prijedor and in Kozarac. You suggested that if the interviewer wanted you to, you could give the names of the persons you had spoken to and who had participated in the conflict that took place in the centre of Kozarac. The first name you mentioned was that of Witness W? 28 A. It is possible that I mentioned that name, but it is just an assumption, only because I knew from earlier that that witness had been in the war in Slavonia, in Zoran Karlica's Unit, and it was common knowledge in Prijedor that Zoran Karlica was Commander of the attack on Kozarac. That is why I thought that he might be one of the participants in the conflict. I did not know for sure whether he really was or not. 7 Q. What you said to Mr. Reid was, "If you want me to, I could give you the names of the persons who had spoken to me and who had participated in the conflict that took place in the centre of Kozarac". Those were your words, not Mr. Reid's, correct? 11 A. Yes, it is possible. It was not a secret. People were talking about the events in Kozarac, but I could not know what was true of all those stories. That was just my assumption. 14 Q. Mr. Tadic, you have spoken in evidence about -- I think I am quoting -- "we simple, ordinary people". The fact is that you were not only a member of the SDS, and not a member in name only, but you were an earnest member of the SDS who before the conflict tried to obtain weapons for Serbs, organise assignments for the conflict, obtain information about weapons which the Muslim police might have and discourage Serbs from co-operating with Muslims? 22 A. That is your opinion. 23 Q. There were people in Kozarac, SDS members, who were not passive members, correct? There were activists, SDS activists, in Kozarac? 26 A. I knew only about my wife and Miso Radulovic. I do not know that there were other members of the SDS during my stay in Kozarac. 1 Q. Miso Radulovic was the man whom you described as an SDS activist? 3 A. It was an assumption. I think it is something that followed from the fact that he was a member -- I think so -- of the board for the plebiscite, nothing else. I am not sure whether he was, but I think he was. 7 Q. Before the conflict in Kozarac, Miso Radulovic tried to organise the assignments for Serbs to be implemented should war break out? 10 A. He talked about the need to evacuate the population, because he used to be a Commander of the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, so he knew about the ways to evacuate population. So in relation to that, it was in relation to that that he talked about the needs and so on, that in case of conflict the population should leave in an organised way, because it was clear to us at that time, me and my family, we were not involved, we were not on the lists for shelters. So everything that followed from my contacts with Miso Radulovic and some other people in Kozarac was in relation to the safety of my family and my personal safety. I tried to create conditions to save me and my family. 21 Q. You worked side by side with Miso Radulovic who was an SDS activist to organise the assignments to be implemented if the war broke out? 24 A. No, I did not work with him about that. Those were just simple conversations. I do not know in what way I was involved, as you say. I do not think he was involved. Those were just discussions, what if this should happen, if that should happen. But nobody had any solutions in that situation. There was a 1 discussion about how to evacuate oneself and one's family. 2 I participated in those discussions because I did not own a car 3 and I knew that I was not on the list of shelters, so I had to 4 talk to someone. Those were just conversations about what to do 5 in this or that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in the report, however, which you prepared and 7 submitted, in the work report which you prepared for the purpose 8 of submitting to SDS officials and other authorities, you 9 described the following: "Under such circumstances, Milos 10 Radulovic and I tried to join forces and organise the 11 assignments to be implemented which, as arranged, were to come 12 into effect should fighting start. The majority of people with 13 the village of Vidovici as a sole exception refused to 14 co-operate siding with the stronger". Those are the words you 15 wrote to, among others, the President of the SDS in Bosnia and 16 Herzegovina to describe what you did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the words that I wrote on the basis of my work as the 18 Secretary of the Local Commune and the reports that had been 19 drafted for the Local Commune in Kozarac in the period 20 of '92, '93. So all that information is based on the 21 declarations and statements of some people who attended those 22 meetings and sessions of the Assembly or the Executive Board. 23 As for those activities, it is normal that I was concerned about 24 how to save me and my family from that area because nobody knew 25 what would happen. So when it comes to co-operation, I talked 26 to Slobodan Savanovic because he had a lorry. I simply needed 27 to have someone if I wanted to leave Kozarac. So I had to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 1 (4.00 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 3 (4.20 p.m.) 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, you may continue. 5 MR. TIEGER: Thank you, your Honour. 6 Q. Mr. Tadic, before the conflict in Kozarac there were sentry posts and checkpoints which were manned by both Serbs and Muslims, is that correct? 9 A. I do not know exactly what period you have -- you are referring to. 11 Q. In 1992, before May 24, when the attack on Kozarac occurred, there were joint checkpoints or joint sentry points in Kozarac? 13 A. I cannot say with certainty that they were joint. I had no particular insight into that. 15 Q. Did you not denounce Serbs who served on checkpoints with Muslims in your letter to the President of the SDS and to others? 18 A. That letter was composed in 1993 and I do not know in what way that was possible to do. I think in '93, I think 8th August '93. 21 Q. You wrote the report on 8th August 1993 and the report encompassed your work for the SDS between the period of time 1990 through 1993, isn't that right? 24 A. Correct, but it is based on information that was in the reports created during the sessions of the Local Communes, presided by Jasikovic Branka, at the -- Bosko Dragicevic presided over the Local Commune and in December of 1992 while I was the President, and so it was based on the statements of the members. Those are -- that is information that is not, that is not verifiable. I was not a policeman to be able to verify it. 3 Q. Mr. Tadic, this report is all about you, is it not? The report begins: "I was born on October 1st 1955 in Kozarac", and it ends with your name, "Dusko Tadic", many pages later? It is about what you did in 1990 through 1993 and it is about your views about what happened during that time? 8 A. In some parts there are elements, my views, but they are all based on my activities in Kozarac, as the Secretary of the Local Commune. I think that the latter part of that report, it states, "The Secretary of the Local Commune". So, as a Secretary, I had access to all the minutes of all meetings of the Assembly of the Local Commune. This was done pretty fast. I was not a typist. There are many mistakes and one -- maybe that was one of the reasons why I was arrested on August 9th when the authorities in Prijedor got a hold of this document. 17 Q. Wherever you got the information about this person from or these people, you write to the SDS authorities that Mirko Grahovac and his son Zeljko were also patrolling at the checkpoint near the Orthodox church and you denounced them for that, isn't that true? 22 A. I do not know how I could denounce in August of '93, a year later in the area of the Local Commune of Kozarac, but that information are facts. 25 Q. Brane Koncar was a Serb who patrolled with Muslims at the checkpoint near the old sawmill and you denounce him for it? 27 A. When you refer to Grahovac, that is only a segment. He stole five or six thousand litres of gasoline while, apparently, he was on duty. I do not know how to take those duties if they were not honest, so this person could have looted all Kozarac. I visited his house. I know what his property was like before the war and what it was after. He had three times more. He had livestock and all of a sudden he had 30 cows. 6 Q. Even before you wrote this letter and even before the outbreak of the conflict, you and Miso Radulovic worked together to discourage Serbs from participating in these joint patrols? 9 A. Those were, perhaps, ideas of Miso, but Miso himself gave his hunting rifle to his colleagues who were manning those checkpoints. It is something that was spoken about. 12 Q. You were trying to persuade Serbs not to participate in the joint checkpoints and joint sentry points? 14 A. After our meeting with the municipal Crisis Staff in Prijedor, we, all of us who were there representing the civic forum, we agreed in every contact with the population, we worked hard on improving the trust in Kozarac. So, regardless of whether somebody was a Muslim, a Serb, if you contacted with friends or acquaintances, we told them how to approach them. We said not to wear a uniform. I still stand by it. I met Emir Susic and I told him, "I will give you my hunting rifle. You should not, and I will -- I do not want you to lose your head". 23 Q. Despite your effort and Miso Radulovic's efforts, Serbs, nevertheless, continued to participate with Muslims in the joint patrols, Serbs like Koncar and Grahovac? 26 A. I do not know if they -- maybe sometimes they, they were seen there, because also Miso's son was on the front line from the first day. I cannot say anything about that. If I talked to 1 Miso about it and Miso himself was present at the Assembly of 2 the Local Commune, and he was talking very strictly to all of us 3 who had these initiatives about Kozarac. He was the Commander 4 of the Territorial Defence of Kozarac. He was a native. He was 5 almost 60 years and I assumed that he had experience. Nobody 6 was under age there, so that I would -- should give them 7 advice. Until the last day, I was socialising with my 9 neighbours, the ones that I trusted and who trusted me. Four 10 days before the conflict, I had a barbecue party with Fikret 11 Tulundzic. We had carp and we barbecued carp, and we looked and 12 we thought that everything would pass. We did not believe that 13 things would happen. I knew that he had weapons; he knew that 14 I had them. He sometimes gave me the bullets for my .765 15 handgun. That was all open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You tried to get other weapons as well; a few months before the 17 war you worked with Vaso Radunjic on trying to get weapons 18 which belonged formerly to the shoe factory and which were 19 stored in the Prijedor barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that event, but I did not take a direct, active 21 part in it. My brother Mladen told me about it, who -- he was 22 in Kozarac four or five months in late '91 and I think my 23 brother was there. He had a van, a Nissan, of red colour. They 24 tried something and nothing came of it. Radunjic was to be 25 fired, he was suspended, and he and his wife who was a Muslim, 26 after the SDA came into power, six months later, he fled 27 abroad. That is only something that I heard. I cannot be sure 28 if that even happened. My brother Mladen could say more about 1 that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let us read the words from the letter which you wrote when you 3 sat down to describe your work for the SDS between 1990 and 4 1993. That is on page 4. "A few months before the war, 5 I worked with Vaso Radunjic, the secretary in resignation in 6 the shoe factory, on trying to get weapons which were the 7 company's property but were stored at the Prijedor barracks. We 8 had delivery documents drafted and an agreement to be allocated 9 those weapons stored at the barracks, but when my brother tried 10 to load them on to the van Captain Javoric in person accompanied 11 by his security officer, Iso, prevented him. It never went any 12 further from that, though news about our attempt leaked down to 13 Kozarac. "I was able to understand the whole thing only when 15 I found out that the security officer mentioned above was a 16 Muslim from Montenegro, and that it was his ethnicity that made 17 our effort futile, though I was never able to understand why 18 Javoric was allowed then and later to work against Serbs, 19 distributing weapons to Muslims and justifying his work by 20 saying that the weapons were common property".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the description is very clear, that Mr. Radunjic, 22 whether he tried or not, I cannot be sure, but on that day I was 23 there. I know that the brother came back to Kozarac and he told 24 about it. Since I have heard of it, about it, I thought that in 25 some ways I was a participant of it. But, as far as Javoric is concerned, I cannot say 27 much. I heard about him before and after the war and there were 28 also stories that he was distributing weapons to everybody, but 1 not to help, but in order to create an even worse situation, 2 only worse. By the very fact that a tank was at the entrance of 4 Kozarac, it was clear that the tank would be used in the 5 conflict in Kozarac. I think it is absurd to think about 6 fighting tanks with rifles. I do not know who could have 7 thought about that. It is already on May 3rd that the Serbs 8 gave clear indications that they would use tanks in Kozarac. I 9 do not know why, how, what an idea it would be had it not been 10 for the conflict. I thought that it would be best if I left 11 Kozarac, and I think that many left before me following the same 12 kind of thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During 1992 you repeatedly attempted to obtain information on 14 the number of weapons that the Kozarac reserve police had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot say -- you could not say that I tried, that there 16 was -- there were always discussions to return the weapons or 17 not. During our meetings in Prijedor it was discussed. There 18 was always arguments, whether they were secret weapons brought 19 in from Sarajevo or whether they were supplying in another way. 20 But none of this information was verified. So, that information seeped into my head as it did 22 into everybody else's. There were a lot of unknowns. My 23 curiosity, if it existed, it was all based on fear for my own 24 personal security. I knew what was to happen. If I had known 25 what was going on, I would have left Kozarac much earlier. Why 26 did I come back, and I would not have taken my family out if 27 I had any other option.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, it is not me who says that you repeatedly attempted to do so. I am just reading from your letter at this point, Mr. Tadic, and I am quoting it on page 4: "When I repeatedly attempted to obtain from him information about the number and nature of weapons the Kozarac reserve police had" -- that is what you wrote in 1993 when you prepared your report about your activities from 1990 to 1993. 7 A. I was curious, that is true, but that is where it stayed. Just as many were curious about whether I had weapons or whether I knew somebody maybe, what was going to happen, but I did not know anything. That was the exchange of views. I do not think that it was anything very significant. 12 Q. Mr. Tadic, you did not engage in these efforts because you were curious or because you were a simple, ordinary person. You did those things because you were an earnest SDS member and a self-proclaimed activist. You describe yourself as an activist in this letter, don't you? 17 A. You could say after August 15 1992 I was, sort of, an activist but nothing before that. 19 Q. You did these things because you were an enthusiastic supporter of the idea of creating Republika Srpska, and that is what you said in this letter? 22 A. Every lay person in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there are three constituent people in Bosnia, Croats, Muslims and Serbs had the equal rights and one of the reasons for my being in -- I lived in a place which was 95 per cent Muslim and I never questioned that. Up until 1992, all my contacts were with my neighbours and in Prijedor I never met with people with whom I had not been meeting before that. All people with whom I was meeting know my 1 views. Had I not been thinking well about people in Prijedor 3 and had I not been thinking well -- meant well for people in 4 Kozarac, I never would have become active in a way I did. 5 Sometimes maybe people joined sentries in order to show to their 6 neighbours how they felt, but I was never in those sentries 7 myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you outlined all these activities to the officials 9 and others whom you intended to receive this letter and you told 10 them how you had worked since 1990 in order to contribute to the 11 creation of a common Serbian country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this letter -- it was created in August, 8th August, 13 1993, and I had been arrested at least 10 times by the 14 authorities that you describe. At the entrance of the city hall 15 in Prijedor, I was again arrested and after that I had to leave 16 Republika Srpska. That is a reflection of my understanding 17 after that letter, that I still had -- that it was still a big 18 tragedy. I had no task. That letter, it was written in a very simple way and 20 it is all based on the Assembly of the Local Commune 21 proceedings. The continuity between 1993, you can see there, 22 there is '93 and then there is 1990. That letter was not 23 directed to the authorities of Republika Srpska. They were only -- I also visited the United Nations office in Belgrade and I 25 talked about that and nobody was really interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After those efforts (some of which you detailed in the letter), 27 when the time came, May 24th, that the Srpski opstina Prijedor 28 would be cleansed of Muslims, you continued to contribute as an 1 activist in places like Omarska, Keraterm and Jaskici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only the contribution to the revival of the Local Commune of 3 Kozarac and, as far as the ethnic cleansing is concerned that 4 you talk about, I do not know what my departure and what the 5 departure of my family from Republika Srpska means, if that is 6 not ethnic cleansing. I did not leave there, because I had it good there 8 because I had some merits, because I thought I left because 9 I did not think that I could really rely on people. I know very 10 well where I was moving. I may be wrong about the dates, that 11 is true. I may be wrong about some descriptions, whether a 12 sleeve was blue or whether the uniform was blue or yellow, but 13 I know where I was all my life. I cannot forget that, and I 14 cannot be wrong whether I was in some location where I had never 15 been in my life. I can be wrong about the date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the cook, the carpenter, the florist, the home maker, the 17 businessman, the school teacher and dozens and dozens and dozens 18 of others from Kozarac, from Kevljani, from Prijedor, from 19 Hrnici, from Jaskici, from Sivci, they are all wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you have in your mind. I do not think that 21 anybody is guilty. Many who came here suffered, but I did too. 22 There is no difference there because I was a Serb and they were 23 Muslims or Croats. All the people who suffered are those who 24 did not want to fight in the Serb Republic on the front line. 25 Those activities were not deemed to anything much in the 26 beginning, those political activities. People who were -- 27 during the communist period everything was taken over from the 28 old system. 1 Q. No, I am talking about the dozens and dozens and dozens of people who saw you in those locations. 3 A. Maybe they saw me in Prijedor. Many of my neighbours whom I saw and with whom I visited, they could see me there. They could see me in Orlovci where I was doing my job. Some of them I even met in Banja Luka, it is true. They could see me on TV images when Monika Gras made her film, and she edited the footage of '91 and puts it in as if it was '92 and then repeats it every week. It was, it was there repeated in Germany every week. My winter uniform and the summer in Trnopolje, that is what she has cut together. So that is the truth. 12 MR. TIEGER: I have nothing further, your Honour. 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: One question, Mr. Tieger, would you go back regarding the certificate that the German authorities showed to Mr. Tadic. You have mentioned a particular Exhibit number and I still want to make it clear in my own mind what certificate we are talking about and whether or not that was shown to Mr. Tadic by the German authorities. 19 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, I read to Mr. Tadic from the text of the interview and that is as far as the testimony went. If the Court has a question about the relationship between the Exhibit number referred to in the German interview ---- 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I will just ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25 Q. Mr. Tadic, the certificate that you have discussed and Mr. Tieger asked you about, and the certificate I am referring to is the one that indicates that you have been issued an automatic rifle and 300 bullets.
