No, it was not shown to me. They described it to me and phrased the question in a way whether I had received it from the Territorial Defence in Banja Luka, "Did you get it as a member of the Territorial Defence Unit?" And I said, "I hear about such certificate for the first time". It was about signing on a weapon. So that is -- and not what my brother gave me which I filled out and which Mr. Prosecutor calls a forgery. 12 Q. So you had not received it from the Territorial Defence, that is what you are saying? You had received it from your brother as you have testified today? 15 A. Yes, the blank certificate and I filled -- I got it from my brother and I knew the number of the rifle and it matches the serial number of the rifle that Kusota signed out on. I think that that can be verified. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger, do you have additional questions in the light of that question? 21 MR. TIEGER: No, your Honour, nothing arising from that. 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, do you have any redirect? 23 MR. KAY: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25 Q. You were asked a series of questions about the interviews with the Prosecutor in May and December 1995 and those were interviews conducted by Mr. Robert Reid. You were asked, or it was put to you, that you had documents there at the time of the interviews. Just so it is clear to us, we have had documents in this Court, but I would like to ask you this: were the lists and the official duty plan that we had produced with the names of people at checkpoint Orlovci as well as the list of names in the schedule with you during that series of interviews in May and December 1995? 7 A. I did not have that document. The one that Mr. Wladimiroff provided, that was given to the Defence. I think that Simo Drljaca was the chief. I had no reason to believe him and so I did not regard that document at all. I was talking about what I tried to remember. 12 Q. Did you have before you during the December or May interview a letter that had been provided by Simo Drljaca? 14 A. No, no, exactly when that took place, there were two pieces of paper with Simo Drljaca's signature and Mr. Wladimiroff put in front of me, and I said that I could use it if I wanted to. I told him that I did not need it and that was sitting next to me. The official documents that I saw, the official working lists, I did not see that. 20 Q. So, the documents that we have had produced in Court showing those on duty at checkpoint Orlovci in the official duty plan as well as the schedule of names with the times and dates were not documents before you during those interviews? 24 A. They were not. 25 Q. I would like you now to look at the work report. If 344A could be provided in your own language before you. 344B, if the Bench have it, is the English translation of that document. Before it goes before you, perhaps if it could be handed to me so that I can find the appropriate passage? If you could look at the text at the top of the page that I am putting before you which is at the foot of page 7 of the English translation? Perhaps if page 7 of the English translation could be put on the overhead monitor? If it could be moved up the screen so we can see the foot of the page? When I raise my hand, if you could turn over to the next page? Mr. Tadic, if you could read out from the top of the that page? I believe it starts: "Fighting in Kozarac started on 25th May 1992". Do you see that at the top? Could you read that what is written in the text there in this work report or letter to Dr. Karadzic? Can you read it out, please, in your own language to us? 14 A. [No interpretation]. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We are not getting any translation. 16 THE WITNESS: "Fighting in Kozarac started on 25th May 1992. One day before that" ---- 18 MR. KAY: Continue. 19 A. "Fighting in Kozarac started on 25th May 1992, and one day before that I had left for Banja Luka where my family lived as refugees in an abandoned house living off of our last saved food. I never took part in the attack on Kozarac because, despite everything after I had been living among those people for 35 years, I still did not see why I would have to shoot at my former neighbours when, surely, things would change with time because the truth will come out and because I did not see that all had to end in destruction and devastation. Mere luck saved those few Serbs who had not been organised and the unexpected chaos in the green berets. I came back to the Kozarac in June of '90 and immediately joined the reserve police force in Prijedor on the traffic police patrol at the checkpoint in Orlovci". 5 Q. Thank you. That is that passage. 6 JUDGE STEPHEN: Does that mean the translation is inaccurate? 7 MR. KAY: No. I am re-examining him on a document that was put before him in relation to his activities at the time. 9 JUDGE STEPHEN: Yes, but there are two lines that appear in the English that were omitted. 11 MR. KAY: I am just going back to that, your Honour, as I was able to notice that as well. 13 JUDGE STEPHEN: Thank you. 14 MR. KAY (To the witness): Could you read it more slowly? I want you to go back to the position of "living among those people for 35 years" which I think you will find is about the fourth line. Just read it slowly, not at 100 miles an hour. 18 A. "I never took part in attack on Kozarac because despite everything, after I had been living among those people for 35 years, I did not see why I would have to shoot at my former neighbours, and in time the truth will come out whether it all had to end up in destruction and devastation, this setting up and looting of people's property, disregarding of who the previous owner was. Mere luck saved those few Serbs who had luck". 26 Q. Just stop there. Can you just go back a sentence and please read it slowly so that the translator can catch your words. Go back to the "35 years" and just read it slowly. Just start at the "35 years". 2 A. "I never took part in the attack on Kozarac because despite everything, after I had been living among those people for 35 years, I thought that I should not shoot at my former neighbours, and that in time the truth will come out whether it all had to end in the destruction and devastation, in setting up camps and looting of property, disregarding of who the previous owner was." 9 Q. Thank you. Your Honour, that is all I ask in re-examination. Great reference has been made in the cross-examination to the two interviews that took place in May and December 1995. I would ask that those be made as Exhibits before the Court in the form of the English translation, so that the Court is able to see the full extent of those interviews. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We have heard a lot of statements and they have been used throughout the trial. I suppose in cross-examination we never received all of the statements though. What is the position of the Prosecutor? Do you have any objection? 19 MR. TIEGER: It had been our intention to tender that document in the course of our rebuttal case, but if the Court wishes it now we do not have any objection. 22 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We will wait until the rebuttal. 23 MR. KAY: I anticipated that was the case as I know Mr. Reid is being called at the rebuttal stage. It just occurred to me it would be useful for the Court to have it now. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It might be better to come in in the orderly way so we can receive the benefit that whoever is going to offer it wishes us to have. Is there anything else? Mr. Kay? 1 MR. KAY: We do not have any witnesses for today, but it looks as though we will get through our business at a fairly early point tomorrow. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: That is what I understand from Mr. Bos. Mr. Tieger, you are standing still, do you want to contribute something or did you have additional questions? I do forget, I am sorry. We got on to other matters about the Exhibit. Do you have any recross, Mr. Tieger? 9 MR. TIEGER: Yes, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 11 Q. Mr. Tadic, with respect to the letter that your counsel referred to when asking you about the rosters and dates, that letter was a timetable of the times and dates at the Orlovci checkpoint, is that correct, the timetable of shifts? 15 A. I do not remember exactly. 16 Q. Well, do you recall that it was a list -- you do not recall the letter at all? 18 A. I remember two pieces. When I saw the signature of Simo Drljaca I left it with my family. I was not interested in that, because I was not sure whether his information was accurate. In view of some previous events I believe that something may be incorrect. 22 Q. Did you not have that document with you during the December 22nd 1995 interview? 24 A. If you allow me, if you show me that, I could tell you. It is not a letter. It is just two pieces of paper. 26 Q. Your Honour, may this be marked for identification as Prosecution next in order? Mr. Tadic, this is the timetable of shifts, among the timetables of shifts which accompanied the letter, correct? 2 A. I have seen this paper, but I do not know which letter you are referring to. It is not clear to me. 4 Q. Well, this is among the documents you had with you on December 22nd 1995 and which you referred to during the course of that interview? 7 A. At one point Mr. Wladimiroff did give me such a sheet of paper with this information, so I had it with me. Yes, this is the document. I just do not think that the signature was the same. I think it was -- yes, timetable of shifts, but the signature was not like this, nor was the stamp. I am not sure. I am not sure if it is the same document. I think there were two sheets of paper, not one. It is not a complete document. 14 Q. There were other dates on there. As you can see that particular document, Exhibit 361, refers to June and July, and the other documents refer to following dates, isn't that true? 17 A. If you say so it must be that way. I just say that I have seen two sheets of paper. I do not know whether this was one of them. I do not remember. I did not pay any attention after that. I just think that it was signed by the Chief of Police, Simo Drljaca. The signature here is Jankovic Mile. I am not sure if this is the paper. If there is another paper I would kindly ask you to give me that paper so I can tell you for certainty whether we are talking about the same thing. 25 Q. May I have this marked as Prosecution Exhibit 362. 26 A. Yes, this is a complete document. This is the form I received and you have here Chief of the Security Services Centre, Simo Drljaca, but I did not have this paper during my interview in Germany and my first interview in The Hague. I did have it at some point during a second interview. Mr. Wladimiroff who had asked one of your members if he could use that, gave me that document and then I had it. I saw the signature Simo Drljaca and I had a look at the document. I just skimmed it and I did not pay any attention to details. 7 Q. May I ask that that document be tendered for admission, your Honour? 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Is there any objection to 361 and 362? 10 MR. KAY: No, your Honour. 11 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: They will be admitted. 12 THE WITNESS: Because here under the paragraph 1 you see that here these are the extracts from timetable of shifts, and at that time we did not have the timetable of shifts available. 15 MR. TIEGER: The ones which were introduced in court? 16 A. Yes. 17 Q. This document is a compilation of those rosters? 18 A. That is what it says here. I did not know whether it -- I did not know whether it was true or not, because here you have an extract from something. 21 Q. Your Honour, I had that marked temporarily as two different Exhibits. I do not think that is appropriate under the circumstances. In addition I would like to have the witness shown this document. 25 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I gather 362, is that for other months, perhaps August and September? 27 MR. TIEGER: This is ---- 28 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: No, 362. 1 MR. TIEGER: Right. One is a letter -- those should be marked, it seems to me, 361A, B and C, and this would be C. 3 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Let us see what this is. 4 MR. TIEGER: Was that part of the document as well? 5 A. It is possible, it is probably that it is, but I cannot claim with certainty when I saw it for the first time. This document is also an extract of something, of a timetable of shifts. So it is a copy of what was written in the police station in Prijedor. The signature is Marko Djinardja. I think that was the person who was Commander of the police station at that time. I was on duty. I was securing the police station in Prijedor and I was also in charge of securing the bus station in Prijedor. 14 Q. Your Honour, I can submit the English translations at the same time. 16 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, is there any objection then to 361 becoming 361A, 362 will become 361B and what now has been marked for identification purposes will be 361C? Do you have any objection? 20 MR. KAY: No objection, your Honour. 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: No objection to the last Exhibit? 22 MR. KAY: No. 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Then they will all be admitted as A, B and C 361. 25 MR. TIEGER: Mr. Tadic, you indicated that you do not recall referring to this document during the course of your interview with Mr. Reid? 28 A. I was told that I could use, I could refer to this document, but I do not remember whether I used it and in what way. 2 Q. Well, do you recall being asked a question about the allegations concerning the 20th, the time period on or around 20th July -- it is page 42 -- then being referred to the document by Mr. Wladimiroff, and then subsequently providing an answer that said: "In any case, I can say that that day I was on duty as a reserve traffic policeman in Orlovci. I was on duty from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m."? Is that something you did without recourse to the document? 10 A. I do not remember. It is also possible that I had a look at the document. I think that his questions were put in such a way that I had to answer whether this was true. That is how I understood it. That was the kind of answer that I gave him, whether it was true or not. At first sight I realised it was not an official document. I knew that there were other documents which are kept in Prijedor. 17 Q. Well, I believe the question on page 41, Mr. Tadic, was: "Is there anything you wish to say in relation to that allegation?" Does such a general question refresh your memory about whether or not you referred to the document yourself in providing such a specific date and time? 22 A. I think that these dates were not especially important in our interview, but it became clear at that moment that there were original documents at that time, and the investigator could go there and check those documents. I only thought that we could talk about whom I spoke and so on at that time. It is perfectly clear how I spent my time there. 28 Q. Mr. Tadic, you wrote your work report in August 1993 and you did so at a time when you were preparing to leave Prijedor, is that right? 3 A. I was not sure whether I was going to leave at that time. It occurred on the 9th, but I was not sure. 5 Q. By that time you were already aware of allegations against you concerning activities in camps and during the cleansing? 7 A. No. I had read some information in Serbian paper Vrema. They were just general allegations in relation to crimes committed. That is what I read in Banja Luka. That information had been sent from Prijedor by the Prijedor authorities in agreement with some journalists, and that is how Mrs. Monika Gras arrived with some policemen to make a video of me in January '93. She could not come to Kozarac without the approval of Mr. Simo Drljaca who finally issued an approval for that, because he knew what he was doing. The subject of Omarska was then simply transferred to Kozarac. 17 Q. You knew this letter was intended to be sent to the media in Yugoslavia and elsewhere? 19 A. That letter should be read from the beginning till the end, and you can easily see that it does not make sense. It relates to a period of three years. I was not a professional. I could not compose a professional letter for the media. That information was taken from the minutes that were available to me at that time. I was being persecuted. I was on the run and that is what I managed to write in a very short period of time. You have many mistakes there. You have very long periods of time. There is a mention of the date of 10th June and so on. So I put zero instead of six. It was not important for me at that moment. I did not think about that at that moment. The essence of what had happened was there. 3 Q. You planned to take this letter with you to Germany where it was ultimately seized from your home? 5 A. No. A lot of documents that you have offered here as evidence against me were found with those papers. If I had thought about that I would have never taken them with me to Germany. I do not know what kind of use I could have with those documents in Germany, I mean, the fact that I had weapons and things like that. I was a persecuted man at that time, ever since the beginning of 1993 until my departure from Yugoslavia. I did not leave because I wanted to leave. 13 Q. This letter was intended to be sent, not to remain in your personal confidential possession as a secret, correct? 15 A. I did not think about that at all. I only remembered about this letter from when the German authorities told me about it. I did not think of any of the documents that I had. I packed within half an hour. I did not have a visa for Germany and it was by sheer luck that I got it through my brother. I left with the Yugoslav selection to Germany. My brother did not send me a guarantee. My brother did not want me to go to Germany and my wife was not there with my brother. She was staying with his former wife and I did not send my wife and my children to my brother's. I had a very bad experience with Serbs, whoever they were. 26 MR. TIEGER: That is all, your Honour. Thank you. 27 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay? 28 MR. KAY: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2 JUDGE STEPHEN: Mr. Tadic, this letter, the work report, did you in fact send one copy off or deliver one copy off to somebody, or did you simply take it with you in your papers? 5 A. When I wrote that letter I made two copies of it. One copy was delivered by me on the same day in Prijedor, and I took the other with me. I left it in my flat in Prijedor. At the time of my arrest on 9th August I just grabbed whatever I could get hold of and fled to Banja Luka. 10 Q. I appreciate that. To whom did you deliver the letter in Prijedor? 12 A. At the very entrance in to Prijedor there is a sort of reception office and I left it there. It is a common procedure if you wanted to hand over any kind of document, if you wanted your document to reach some authority. 16 Q. Yes. At the very entrance to what? You say "at the very entrance"? 18 A. To the town hall in Prijedor. 19 Q. The Monika Gras interview with you which was made into a film, when did that occur, about? 21 A. I know. I remember that event very well. On 31st December in '92 I was in Belgrade. I was there for the New Year's Eve. I came back and I was surprised to learn. At the beginning of '93 in January I went to my work, my work as the Secretary of the Local Commune in Kozarac, and all of a sudden I saw just across the church a TV team and Monika Gras, whose name I learned later on, were there together with two policemen from Prijedor. They were talking to Dusanka, I do not her surname but at that she was working as a teleographer (?) in the Prijedor police station. At one she said: "They are looking for you. They want to talk to you." I said: "Why to me?" They explained that they had come to Prijedor under somebody's instructions and the Commander had sent them there. I did not know what it was all about, and Dusanka told me: "They are talking about the church. They do not believe that it is 120 years old church", and so on. I told them that I did not want to talk to such people, because I did not know what the conversation would be about. 11 Q. But I only wanted to know the date and you have told me that. One other thing I wanted to know about it. Did the film accuse you of acts similar to some of those in the present indictment? 14 A. Yes, and partly the text and the warrant of arrest, that was publicly declared by Emin Jakupovic on TV and some other people. It was obviously a suggestion of Monika Gras. They kept saying "Dule, Dule, Dule". There was a big montage which showed my image at that time. They were filming me and I was not aware of that fact. 20 Q. I think that at one stage in your evidence you mentioned somebody by the name of Cirkin, and I think that you referred to him as having a criminal record. Am I right in the name? 23 A. Yes. 24 Q. Is that the same person as the Captain Cirkin that we, long ago now, in evidence heard had been organising Muslim resistance, or is it a different person altogether? 27 A. It is a different person. I now remember the name. His name was Ramiz Cirkin. He had spent many years in prison and he was well-known in that area. 2 Q. If it is a different person ---- 3 A. It is not the same person. 4 Q. If it is not the same person I am not interested. The next thing I wanted to ask you was about the checkpoint at Orlovci. We have heard a lot about caravans, containers. You spoke about caravans. Initially there was nothing. Then there was a caravan. At any time were there two containers beside the checkpoint? 10 A. It is quite possible. To be frank, I cannot say with certainty because we did not pay much attention to that vehicle. We never really used them. They belonged to the military police. They had their instructions about that. They did what they wanted with that. It is possible. We mainly used our vehicles, vehicles which belonged to the police, because we had a radio connection from the car. 17 Q. The final question I wanted to ask you was, you said, I think, that the real reason for your frequent arrests by the military police in 1993 was not a question, as I had perhaps earlier gathered, of rivalry over the ownership of a cafe or the operation of a cafe in Prijedor, but there was another real reason. What was that real reason? 23 A. For a very long time I thought that the cafe was the reason and my family thought so. However, when I publicly stated that I would not use that cafe, those business premises, I had adapted it and so on, but it would have been absurd for me to enter into any kind of business at that time because the military had the power at that time. But after several arrests took place I realised that that was not the case, because they knew that the cafe was no longer a problem. The real reason I think was the fact that I had become involved in the revival of Kozarac. They did not want Kozarac, life to be brought back to Kozarac, and they did everything they could not to revive that town. 7 Q. Who is "they"? 8 A. It was only later that I understood. The municipal Crisis Staff had an absolute power. They were above everyone else, above the Regional Crisis Staff and the area of Kozarac at that time was under the jurisdiction of the Regional Crisis Staff in Lamovita. We were just mocked by people from the Regional Crisis Staff. We were insignificant. 14 JUDGE STEPHEN: Thank you. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Additional questions, Mr. Kay? 16 MR. KAY: No, thank you, your Honour. 17 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger? 18 MR. TIEGER: Your Honour, if I could just have a second. Thank you your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21 Q. Mr. Tadic, you mentioned that you intended to drop the letter off for a municipal official in Prijedor. Who was that official? 24 A. I do not know with whom I left it. I did not think about that. I know that in the town hall there were some authorities like in any other town hall, but it was not any specific individual and I did not believe that it would end up in the hands of Karadzic, as you stated. If it had ended up in his hands I would not have been arrested maybe. 2 Q. You said you went to Germany as part of the Yugoslav selection. What did you mean by that? 4 A. I was not a member of the Yugoslav selection. My brother was very influential, a karate sportsman, and very often he was the host of the Yugoslav selection in karate in Germany. So he had intervened with the then President of the karate association and he asked him to help me with the visa, because I had no other opportunity to go to Germany. So I was some kind of -- I accompanied the selection, the karate selection of Yugoslavia at that time. 12 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay? 13 MR. KAY: No thank you, your Honour. 14 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Just one question. Mr. Tadic you just indicated that you did not know the person whom you left the letter with at the reception centre. But who was the official to whom you wanted this letter delivered? 18 A. I did not have any specific person in mind. I was just thinking of someone who could help me and who could check those data. I did not think about that. If I had thought about that I would have sent it maybe to the Chief of Police as any ordinary citizen would do. I did not have a clear idea in my mind about what to do with it. 24 Q. So you left it with the reception centre in Prijedor, at the town hall? 26 A. Yes. 27 Q. Did you leave it in an envelope with anyone's name on it or did you just leave it with the receptionist? 1 A. It was in an envelope. I just left it there. I put "Municipal" ---- 3 Q. Municipal? 4 A. --- "Assembly Prijedor". 5 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, additional questions? 6 MR. KAY: No thank you, your Honour. 7 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tieger? 8 MR. TIEGER: No thank you, your Honour. 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Tadic, I presume will be excused. You will be with us. My usual question is, is there any objection to the witness being permanently excused. I am sure you have heard me say that for several months now. So I do not have to say that today. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10. I understand from Mr. Bos that you expect you will be finishing tomorrow with your case in chief? 16 MR. KAY: Yes, your Honour. 17 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Very good. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10 a.m. 19 (5.30 p.m.) (The court adjourned until the following day).
